transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 14:05 PST | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Solutions); Alex Kim (Peregrine Head of ML), Jordan Blake (Infra), Ravi Patel (Finance)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on unit economics across Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Peregrine wants to understand per-token costs, how batching and KV/prefix caching affect unit cost, and what predictable budgeting looks like with Reserved/Dedicated capacity. They flagged compliance and deployment flexibility as secondary constraints.

Topics:
- current stack and inference patterns
- expected qps, average/peak context lengths
- cost per token sensitivity and batching/caching levers
- reserved capacity vs hosted burst model and invoicing
- compliance (SOC2, VPC, KMS)
- next steps for pilot/benchmark

Action items (recorded in-call): Maya to send pricing + example cost model spreadsheet; Diego to run bench plan; Alex to share prompt samples and daily token estimates.

Transcript:
00:00:05 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um Alex, Jordan, Ravi from Peregrine, thanks for making time. We're gonna run through cost economics, quick Q on your current infra before we jump in.
00:00:14 Alex Kim: Yeah thanks Maya. Um to start, we are currently running most inference on a hybrid setup, small in-house Triton endpoints for low-latency pieces and then we burst to a managed provider for larger generation tasks. We're trying to figure out if moving to Redwood Hosted or grabbing Dedicated makes sense economically.
00:00:30 Diego Alvarez: Got it. Can you share peak qps and average context length? Those are big drivers for batching and KV caching benefits.
00:00:38 Alex Kim: Average context is around 1.2k tokens, but we have a fat tail up to 6k for long reports. Peak qps is roughly 50 requests/sec during market open windows, baseline 10 qps otherwise.
00:00:52 Jordan Blake: Also important — we have a hard monthly budget cap from finance, so predictable monthly unit costs help us. We can't get surprised by big token spikes.
00:01:01 Ravi Patel: Yep, we have a $60k/month pilot budget allocated for next quarter. Need to understand if that covers a hosted approach or if we need to commit to Dedicated to hit throughput and price targets.
00:01:12 Priya Nair: Thanks — good context. Quick framing: Hosted gives simple per-token billing with no infra commitment; Dedicated is reserved capacity with a monthly commit that yields lower per-token cost and predictable unit economics; Private adds more control and an enterprise license. We can model both.
00:01:27 Diego Alvarez: On the technical side, two levers materially change cost per effective token: batching across inflight requests and KV/prefix caching for repeated context. For your workload with long doc summaries, prefix caching could reduce tokens sent to model by 30-70% depending on reuse patterns. Batching can improve GPU utilization and lower per-token GPU time by roughly 20-50% depending on latency SLOs.
00:01:48 Alex Kim: When you say 30-70% for caching, is that from our historical reuse or you're quoting general numbers?
00:01:54 Diego Alvarez: General ranges — with Peregrine's long-report use, if you have stable instructions or long shared preamble across requests, we've seen 40-60% token reduction in similar customers. But we need your prompt set to simulate.
00:02:06 Maya Chen: On pricing, high-level hosted numbers we quoted in the deck: for generation models X (open-ish) we'd be in the few tenths of a cent per 1k tokens range — again these are ballpark and depend on model, quantization and whether you hit batching/caching improvements.
00:02:25 Ravi Patel: Can you give an example calc? Say we have 50k generated tokens/day raw, how does caching + batching move the monthly bill?
00:02:33 Diego Alvarez: Sure — quick napkin: 50k tokens/day -> 1.5M tokens/month raw. If caching reduces tokens by 40% that's 900k effective tokens/month. Batching gains improve GPU efficiency; maybe we can treat that as a 20% cost reduction on top of the token reduction, leading to effective cost ~900k * 0.8 = 720k token-equivalent units. Multiply by hosted per-token price to get cost. If hosted is $0.0008 per token equivalent (example), that's about $576/month. With Dedicated we often see unit economics improve another 30-50% because reserved infra is cheaper per-GPU-hour and we can tune quantization and kernel selection to lower cost, so maybe $300-$400/month.
00:03:06 Jordan Blake: Wait, those hosted numbers feel low — we're used to seeing higher per-token costs from other providers for long sequences, and our current in-house costs are different because we amortize infra. Also we care about latency SLOs, can't batch too aggressively during market windows.
00:03:20 Diego Alvarez: Totally — latency windows reduce batching headroom. Our runtime has continuous batching that respects per-request latency SLOs so you don't block on batch formation. The cost model should explicitly model percent of time in high-latency-tolerance vs low-latency windows.
00:03:33 Alex Kim: What's the onboarding like for Dedicated? Do we need to commit months upfront? What's the elasticity if we under/over provision?
00:03:40 Maya Chen: Dedicated is backed by a monthly commit; you can choose reserved pool size and autoscaling/burst policies. We do quarterly/annual contracts; there's also a hybrid where you run Hosted normally and spin up Dedicated for predictable windows. Billing is straightforward — monthly invoice for reserved capacity plus overage/usage rules we can lay out.
00:03:56 Ravi Patel: For budget planning, we need an example: with our $60k pilot and expected 1.5M raw tokens/month, what scenario fits?
00:04:04 Diego Alvarez: With 1.5M raw/month and conservative 30% caching and 15% batching uplift, you're at ~892k effective tokens. Multiply by hosted per-token example $0.0009 gives ~$803/month, so $60k easily covers pilot. But if you want Dedicated to shave more, the threshold where Dedicated commits make sense is when you have sustained high throughput where reserved GPU amortization reduces unit cost materially — often useful above tens of millions tokens/month, but depends on the model and quantization profile.
00:04:36 Alex Kim: That threshold seems high. Our medium-term plan could ramp to 20-30M tokens/month, at which point Dedicated probably makes sense.
00:04:43 Priya Nair: Exactly — we can build a simple model for you with your ramp profile. We'll include sensitivity to caching % and batching allowed latency.
00:04:52 Jordan Blake: Another technical Q: how do you handle KV cache consistency for private deployments? We have some legal/regulatory constraints on ephemeral keys and wanting to keep embedding caches on-prem.
00:05:01 Diego Alvarez: For Redwood Private we can run the inference runtime in your VPC/on-prem; KV cache can be configured to stay inside the customer network. For Hosted, KV is ephemeral and can be configured with TTLs; we also have options to encrypt in transit and at rest with customer-managed KMS for dedicated/private.
00:05:18 Alex Kim: Good — SOC2 and SSO are checkboxes, but the KMS angle is important. Also any additional fees for private?
00:05:23 Maya Chen: Private includes a platform license and implementation/support fees. We'll outline typical T&Cs in a proposal.
00:05:29 Ravi Patel: Back to competitive comparison — how does Redwood compare to OpenAI or Anthropic for unit cost? We're currently benchmarking both.
00:05:36 Diego Alvarez: We focus on production economics: our runtime + batching/caching + dedicated reserved pools typically deliver better per-token economics vs API-only providers at scale, especially when you can use model quantization or specialized kernels. For small scale, per-token on Hosted might be comparable, but the levers for optimization are more limited on closed APIs.
00:05:53 Alex Kim: OK. Last set of items: can you run a bench with our prompts? We'd like to see latency percentiles and cost per effective token with caching/batching toggled.
00:06:03 Diego Alvarez: Yes — suggested plan: you provide representative prompt set and traffic shape; we'll run three configs: Hosted baseline, Dedicated reserved pool, and Dedicated with aggressive KV caching + lower-precision quantization. We'll return latency p50/p95 and cost per effective token.
00:06:17 Maya Chen: For next steps, we'll send a pricing spreadsheet that you can edit with your numbers. Diego will propose the bench run plan and required sample payload format. Alex, if you can share prompts and a typical 2-week traffic trace that would be ideal.
00:06:29 Alex Kim: Will do. I'll share a sanitized prompt set and synthetic trace by Monday.
00:06:33 Ravi Patel: And I'll review the pricing model to make sure it fits the $60k cap and flag if we need to move toward a short Dedicated pilot.
00:06:40 Maya Chen: Great, thanks all. Any final Qs?
00:06:44 Jordan Blake: One small thing — p95 latency requirement during market open is 300ms or we can't batch much. Is that realistically achievable with long context?
00:06:52 Diego Alvarez: 300ms p95 for 6k context is very tight; we'd likely need smaller model variants or aggressive sharding. For some workloads we do hybrid: quick short-context models for market-critical ops and larger models for off-hours or async processing. We'll call that out in the bench.
00:07:08 Maya Chen: Okay wrapping up — recapping action items and we'll follow up with calendar invite for the technical deep dive. Thanks everyone.

End of meeting.
